stages.topic: How to Make Money on Instagram: Every Way Creators Get Paid
stages.brief:
I've finished the research and written the brief below. The main gap: I couldn't read Instagram's Help Center or Partner Monetization Policies pages, because they need JavaScript. So the follower minimums for Subscriptions (10K) and Gifts (500) come only from Buffer and Wix, not from Instagram. The writer has to name those sources and tell readers to check eligibility in their own app.

# Content brief: How to make money on Instagram

## 1. Chosen query and intent
- **Chosen query:** how to make money on instagram (the only candidate; its demand is obvious from who ranks for it)
- **Focus keyphrase:** how to make money on Instagram
- **Search intent:** An informational list of options with some how-to. The results ranking now are "X ways" lists: Buffer (12 ways), Wix (12), Printful (14), Outfy (11), Network Solutions (11) and Oberlo. Readers want every option, how much following each needs, and how the money reaches them.
- **Suggested title:** How to Make Money on Instagram: Every Way Creators Get Paid, Who Pays You, and What Each Needs

## 2. Unique angle (what we add)
1. **Sort by who pays you, not a flat list of 12.** There are four groups: fans paying through Instagram (Subscriptions, Gifts, Badges), Instagram itself (Bonuses), brands (sponsored posts, partnership ads, affiliate links, UGC), and your own customers (products and services). Instagram's creator site uses a similar split ("Earn from audience / Earn from brands / Earn from Instagram").
2. **A decision table.** For each method: what you need to start, who takes a cut, when you're paid, and what you must disclose. Only sourced cells get filled in; anything else says "not published / varies, check your dashboard."
3. **Fixes errors in the top results.** Wix still quotes Zuckerberg's 2021 promise to keep fees free "until 2023." We use the fee wording on Instagram's own Badges page instead. Buffer gives per-view bonus rates and per-post rates from third parties; we leave those out because we can't source them.
4. **A practical disclosure section.** It uses the FTC's own wording, including that free products count as payment, and Instagram's rule that gifted products need the Paid Partnership label.
5. **A tax note** from the IRS: platform income is taxable even without a 1099.
6. **No first-person testing** (Buffer's article relies on "I tried it"). Ours is written as a guide.

## 3. Outline (H2/H3)
**Intro (2–3 sentences):** Use the keyphrase once. Say directly that most Instagram income comes from brands and your own customers, not from Instagram, and that in-app tools have eligibility rules that vary by country.

**H2: The four ways money reaches you on Instagram**
Short overview of the four groups (fans, Instagram, brands, customers).

**H2: Quick comparison: what each method needs and who takes a cut**
The decision table. Columns: Method | Who pays | What you need to start | Fees or cut | When you're paid | Disclosure needed?

**H2: Getting paid by your followers inside Instagram**
- H3: Subscriptions (monthly fee, exclusive content)
- H3: Gifts on Reels
- H3: Badges during Live
- H3: Eligibility rules that apply to all three (18+, professional account, monetization policies, supported country). Frame these as reported by Buffer and Wix; tell readers to check in the app.

**H2: Bonuses: when Instagram pays you directly**
Invite-only and limited-time. No guaranteed rates.

**H2: Getting paid by brands**
- H3: Sponsored posts and how to price them (bring data: followers, average likes, views, comments, shares)
- H3: Finding brands: Instagram's Creator Marketplace, pitching directly, and other matchmaking marketplaces. **Product mention here (see section 6).**
- H3: Partnership ads: ask for higher pay when a brand runs your post as an ad
- H3: Affiliate links and UGC (no in-app minimum; explain the model only, no Instagram feature claims)

**H2: Selling your own products and services**
Courses, templates, services, merch, coaching. Instagram is the shop window and payment happens elsewhere. Don't describe Instagram Shop eligibility or steps, since we have no official source.

**H2: Disclosing paid posts: Instagram's label and FTC rules**
What counts as payment, where the disclosure goes, which words to use and which to avoid.

**H2: Taxes on Instagram income**
IRS gig-economy points.

**H2: Which path to start with**
A short scenario list based on facts above, e.g. "Under the reported thresholds: brands, affiliate and your own products. Over 10K in a supported country: add Subscriptions." No invented income figures.

**FAQ (optional):** Does Instagram pay for views? (Only through invite-only Bonuses.) Do I need a big following? (Answer with the attributed thresholds.)

## 4. Facts to use (with URLs)
**Official Instagram (creators.instagram.com, pages undated):**
- **F1. Bonuses:** "Bonuses are limited time and invite-only as we build toward a sustainable program." They reward performance of reels, carousels and single image posts. https://creators.instagram.com/earn-money/bonuses
- **F2. Subscriptions:** Subscribers pay a monthly fee to see exclusive content marked with a purple ring and get a subscriber badge. The creator sets the price and can change it later in subscription settings. Payouts arrive on the 21st of the following month ("payouts for earnings in the month of March will be paid out on April 21st"). https://creators.instagram.com/earn-money/subscriptions
- **F3. Gifts:** People buy Stars and send virtual gifts on Reels they like. https://creators.instagram.com/earn-money/gifts
- **F4. Badges:** Viewers buy badges during Live in $0.99, $1.99 and $4.99 amounts, up to USD $250 per live video. You're paid once you've earned at least $100, and the money takes 1–7 business days depending on your bank. "Google and Apple deduct 30% of all in-app purchases in fees. Currently Instagram receives no portion of the fees." https://creators.instagram.com/earn-money/badges
  - Undated vendor page. Write it as "Instagram's Badges page says…"
  - The 30% figure is stated for Badges only. Don't apply it to Subscriptions or Gifts.
- **F5. Branded content / Creator Marketplace:**
  - Creator Marketplace is presented as a way to "get discovered by brands."
  - "If you're getting paid in any form for your content, you'll need to add a Paid Partnership label."
  - Free trips and gifted products count: "anything received from business partners counts, whether it be money or otherwise."
  - Some categories are prohibited (drugs, weapons) and some are restricted (alcohol).
  - No pre-, mid- or post-roll ads or banner ads inside your content.
  - Terms are negotiated per deal. Bring data such as followers and average likes, views, comments and shares.
  - Source: https://creators.instagram.com/earn-money/creator-marketplace
- **F6. Partnership ads:** Brands run your content as an ad to reach people beyond both accounts' followers, so "you can advocate for higher pay given the extended usage rights." Reels, stories, static posts and carousels can all be used. Content with licensed music can't run as a partnership ad. You must give ad permissions. https://creators.instagram.com/earn-money/partnership-ads
- **F7. Mixing tools:** Instagram suggests combining tools: "There's no one-size-fits-all approach to making money on Instagram." https://creators.instagram.com/earn-cash-making-what-you-love

**FTC (published 2019-10-24, modified 2024-12-03, footer "November 2019"):** https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/disclosures-101-social-media-influencers
- **F8.** You must disclose any financial, employment, personal or family relationship with a brand. Free or discounted products count.
- **F9.** Put the disclosure with the endorsement, not only in the bio, behind "more", or among hashtags. In Stories, place it over the image. In video, put it in the video itself. On Live, repeat it.
- **F10.** "Ad", "advertisement" and "sponsored" work. Avoid "sp", "spon", "collab" and a stand-alone "thanks" or "ambassador". Don't rely only on a platform's disclosure tool.
- **F11.** U.S. law applies to posts made abroad "if it's reasonably foreseeable that the post will affect U.S. consumers."

**IRS:** https://www.irs.gov/businesses/gig-economy-tax-center (undated)
- **F12.** Gig and platform income must be reported even if it is part-time, not on a 1099 or W-2, or paid in property, goods or virtual currency. "Provide creative or professional services" and "Sell goods online" are listed as gig work. Apply this to U.S. readers only.

**Secondary sources (always attribute):**
- **F13. Subscriptions:** Professional account, at least 10K followers, age 18+, supported country, and you must meet the Content Monetization and Partner Monetization policies. Not available to accounts that mainly post content focused on children. Buffer, on-page date April 23, 2026: https://buffer.com/resources/how-to-make-money-on-instagram/
  - Wix (May 14, 2026, updated Oct 18, 2026) agrees on Professional account, 10,000 followers and supported country, and gives a price range of $0.99–$99.99: https://www.wix.com/blog/how-to-make-money-on-instagram
  - Use the price range only if attributed to Wix, or leave it out.
- **F14. Gifts:** Professional account, 500+ followers, select countries. Buffer, same URL. Buffer's star value ($0.01) and $25 payout minimum appear only in Buffer; leave them out or attribute them clearly.
- **F15.** Buffer: thresholds "may vary by region and over time." Brand deals, UGC and affiliate work "have no minimum" (that is Buffer's statement).
- **F16. Creator Marketplace:** You must be 18+ and follow the Partner Monetization Policies, Community Guidelines and Content Monetization Policies. Wix, URL above.

**Don't use:** Buffer's per-view bonus rates, the nano-influencer rates (which Buffer takes from Influencer Marketing Hub, not read), the Mosseri quote (only seen second-hand), the "80% of people…" stat on Wix, and Wix's statements about the 2023 fee waiver.

## 5. Internal links
- The section on Gifts and Badges paying through in-app purchases links to "How Much Does YouTube Pay per View?" and "TikTok Creator Rewards Program" for comparison.
- The media-kit and audience-data step in the brand section links to "Instagram Follower Location: How to See Which Countries and Cities Your Followers Are From."
- The tip on posting consistently for gifts and bonuses links to "Best Time to Post on Instagram."
- The section on selling your own products links to "How to Make Money on Pinterest Without a Big Following" and "Print on Demand for Beginners" (for merch).
- The tax section links to "Passive Income vs Active Income" (IRS definitions).
- A one-line pointer to other channels links to "How to Make Money Online: 5 Ways and What Each Platform Takes."

## 6. Product link (Instagramaps): justified, one or two mentions
- **Where it goes:** the H3 on finding brands and pricing sponsored posts.
- **Why:** Instagram itself tells creators to bring data when negotiating (F5). Instagramaps "lets creators and businesses connect an Instagram account to see where their audience engages by country and city" and "compares views, reach and engagement per post." It also "includes a marketplace where creators and businesses create profiles, get matched and send collaboration requests," which belongs next to Instagram's own Creator Marketplace.
- **Price wording:** "has free Creator and Business plans; paid plans start at 9 USD per month (check the pricing page for current prices)."
- **Rules:** Link https://instagramaps.com/ at most twice. Present it as one option alongside Creator Marketplace, and don't compare it to other tools.

## 7. Notes for the writer
- Instagram's settings can differ by country, app version and account. Say this wherever you mention dashboard steps, and give no exact tap-paths.
- Use the keyphrase in the title, the intro and once or twice more. Don't put it in every heading.

---

article.title: How to Make Money on Instagram: Every Way Creators Get Paid, Who Pays You, and What Each Needs
article.seo_title: How to Make Money on Instagram: Who Pays and What It Takes
article.meta_description: How to make money on Instagram, sorted by who pays you: fans, Instagram, brands or your customers. Requirements, fees, payout timing and FTC disclosure rules.
article.focus_keyphrase: how to make money on Instagram
article.excerpt: Instagram income comes from four places: fans paying in the app, invite-only Bonuses, brands, and your own customers. Here is what each option needs, who takes a cut, when you get paid, and what you must disclose.
article.content_html:
The first step in working out how to make money on Instagram is knowing who actually pays you. Instagram pays creators directly only through Bonuses, which its own page describes as limited time and invite-only. Every other option is money from fans buying inside the app, from brands, or from your own customers. The in-app tools have eligibility rules that, as Buffer notes, may vary by region and over time.

The four ways money reaches you on Instagram

Instagram's creator site says "There's no one-size-fits-all approach to making money on Instagram" and suggests you can use Subscriptions, Gifts and brand partnerships at the same time. Sorting the options by who pays makes it easier to see which ones fit your account today:

  1. Your followers, inside Instagram: Subscriptions, Gifts on Reels and Badges during Live.
  2. Instagram itself: Bonuses, by invitation only.
  3. Brands: sponsored posts, partnership ads, affiliate links and user-generated content (UGC).
  4. Your own customers: products and services you sell, with Instagram as the place people find you.

If you are comparing Instagram with other channels, our guide to how to make money online and what each platform takes covers the wider picture.

Quick comparison: what each method needs and who takes a cut

Cells marked "not published" mean none of the sources we read state it. Check your own account before you plan around any of these.

MethodWho paysWhat you need to startFees or cutWhen you're paidDisclosure needed?
SubscriptionsFollowers, monthlyProfessional account, at least 10K followers, 18+, supported country, per BufferNot published on Instagram's Subscriptions page; check your settingsOn the 21st of the following month, per InstagramOnly if the content involves a brand relationship
Gifts on ReelsViewers who buy StarsProfessional account, 500+ followers, select countries, per BufferNot published on Instagram's Gifts pageNot published; check in the appOnly if the content involves a brand relationship
Badges on LiveLive viewersEligibility not listed in our sources; check in the appGoogle and Apple deduct 30% of in-app purchases; Instagram says it currently receives no portion, per its Badges pageOnce you've earned at least $100, then 1–7 business days depending on your bank (Instagram)Only if the Live involves a brand relationship
BonusesInstagramAn invitation; Buffer says you need a payout accountNot publishedNot published; check your dashboardNo brand involved
Sponsored postsBrandsNo minimum, per BufferNegotiated per dealAgreed in your contractYes: Paid Partnership label plus a clear disclosure
Partnership adsBrandsAd permissions granted; no licensed musicNegotiated; ask for more for ad usageAgreed in your contractYes
Affiliate linksBrands or affiliate programsNo minimum, per BufferSet by each programSet by each programYes: it's a financial relationship
UGCBrandsNo minimum, per BufferNegotiatedAgreed in your contractYes, if you also post it on your account
Your own products and servicesYour customersSomething to sell and a way to take paymentSet by your store or payment platformSet by your store or payment platformNot a brand deal, but make clear it's your product

Getting paid by your followers inside Instagram

Subscriptions

According to Instagram's Subscriptions page, subscribers pay a monthly fee to see exclusive content highlighted with a purple ring, and they get a subscriber badge next to their name in comments and DMs. You set the price, and you can change it later in the subscription settings. Wix reports that the price can be set anywhere from $0.99 to $99.99 a month; check the options your own app shows.

Payouts arrive on the 21st of the following month. Instagram's example: earnings from March are paid on April 21 (source). That gap matters if you are counting on the money for bills.

Before you switch Subscriptions on, write down what subscribers will get each week, for example a weekly breakdown post, a monthly tutorial or early access to content you would otherwise post publicly. People are paying every month, so plan exclusive content you can keep producing.

Gifts on Reels

Instagram's Gifts page says people can purchase Stars and share virtual gifts in the app to show appreciation for Reels they love. That page doesn't list eligibility criteria or a payout rate. Buffer reports that Gifts are offered to creators with a professional account and at least 500 followers, in selected countries only.

Because Gifts are tied to Reels, they only make sense if you publish Reels regularly. Our guide to the best time to post on Instagram shows how to find the posting times that suit your audience.

Badges during Live

Instagram's Badges page says viewers can buy badges during your Live in $0.99, $1.99 and $4.99 increments, up to USD $250 per live video. You get paid once you've earned at least $100, and the money then takes 1–7 business days to arrive, depending on your bank.

On fees, the same page says: "Google and Apple deduct 30% of all in-app purchases in fees. Currently Instagram receives no portion of the fees." That statement appears on the Badges page only, and the word "currently" means it can change. Don't assume the same split applies to Subscriptions or Gifts; check the earnings details in your own account.

If you want to compare in-app tipping and payouts with other platforms, see how much YouTube pays per view and our breakdown of the TikTok Creator Rewards Program.

Eligibility rules that apply to all three

Instagram's own Subscriptions and Gifts pages don't list who qualifies, so the thresholds in this guide come from secondary sources. For Subscriptions, Buffer lists these requirements (source):

  • Be at least 18.
  • Have a professional Instagram account with at least 10K followers.
  • Live in a country where the feature is available.
  • Have a profile that meets Instagram's Content Monetization and Partner Monetization policies.
  • Not mainly post content focused on children; Buffer says Subscriptions aren't available to those accounts.

Wix agrees on a Professional account, at least 10,000 followers and a supported country. Buffer adds that these thresholds may vary by region and over time. Instagram's menus also differ by country, app version and account type, so treat what your own app shows as the final word. If a feature doesn't appear for you, it isn't available to your account yet.

Bonuses: when Instagram pays you directly

Instagram says Bonuses reward the performance of your reels and photos, including carousels and single image posts, and that they are "limited time and invite-only as we build toward a sustainable program" (source). Wix also describes them as currently invite-only.

You can't apply. If you are invited, Buffer notes that you must add a payout account to receive a bonus payout. Instagram doesn't publish rates in the sources we read, so treat any Bonus as extra money, not as income you plan around.

Getting paid by brands

Sponsored posts and how to price them

Instagram says you'll negotiate the terms of every branded content deal, so each one will be different. It suggests giving the brand data such as your number of followers and your average likes, views, comments and shares (source). Put that into a one-page media kit:

  1. Who you are: handle, niche and the kind of content you make.
  2. Your numbers: followers, plus average likes, views, comments and shares across recent posts. Use averages rather than your single best post.
  3. Where your audience is: if a brand only sells in certain countries, show where your followers are. Our guide to Instagram follower location explains how to find this.
  4. What you offer: list deliverables separately, for example one Reel, three Stories, or a carousel.
  5. Usage terms: say whether the brand can run your post as an ad, and price that separately (see partnership ads below).

We don't quote per-post rates here, because we couldn't find a source we could verify. Build your quote from your deliverables and your data, and adjust after each deal.

Finding brands

There are three main routes:

  • Instagram's Creator Marketplace. Instagram presents it as a way for creators to get discovered by brands. Wix reports that to join, creators must be 18 or older and follow Instagram's Partner Monetization Policies, Community Guidelines and Content Monetization Policies.
  • Pitching directly. Start with brands you already buy and mention. Send a short message with one specific content idea, your deliverables and your media kit numbers.
  • Other matchmaking marketplaces. These let you create a profile and receive or send collaboration requests outside Instagram.

One option for the last route is Instagramaps. It includes a marketplace where creators and businesses create profiles, get matched and send collaboration requests. It also lets you connect an Instagram account to see where your audience engages by country and city, and compares views, reach and engagement per post, which is the kind of data Instagram suggests you bring to a negotiation. It has free Creator and Business plans, and paid plans start at 9 USD per month (check the pricing page for current prices).

Disclosure: Instagramaps is built by the team behind New Earns. We mention it where it fits the task; the steps in this guide also work with other tools.

Partnership ads: ask for more when a brand runs your post as an ad

With partnership ads, brands run your content as an ad to reach people beyond your followers. Instagram says that because the brand puts money behind your content, "you can advocate for higher pay given the extended usage rights" (source).

  • Reels, stories, static posts and carousels can all be run as partnership ads.
  • Content that includes licensed music can't be run as a partnership ad.
  • You need to give ad permissions before the brand can promote your post.
  • If you post first and the brand boosts it, the post shows on your grid. If you send the content to the brand to upload through Ads Manager, it doesn't.

In practice: ask early whether the brand plans to run your content as an ad, quote ad usage as a separate line, and agree whether the post should appear on your grid.

Affiliate links and UGC

Buffer notes that brand deals, UGC work and affiliate marketing have no minimum follower count, which makes them the usual starting point for smaller accounts.

  • Affiliate marketing: you join a brand's or retailer's affiliate program, share a tracked link or code, and earn a commission when people buy. Commission rates and payout rules are set by each program, so read its terms before you promote.
  • UGC: a brand pays you to make photos or videos that it posts on its own channels or uses in its ads. Your follower count matters less than the quality of the content, so a small portfolio of sample videos does most of the selling.

Selling your own products and services

Your own offer doesn't depend on Instagram's monetization rules. Common options include courses, templates, coaching, freelance services such as editing or photography, and merch. In this model Instagram is the shop window: you show your work in posts, Reels and Stories, then send people to wherever you take payment, such as your own website or a third-party store. Each store or payment platform sets its own fees, so check their pricing pages.

  1. Pick one offer that matches what people already ask you about in comments or DMs.
  2. Set up checkout on a platform you control.
  3. Post content that shows the result your product delivers, and point to the purchase link.
  4. Answer questions in DMs and turn the common ones into posts.

If you want to sell merch without holding stock, see print on demand for beginners. For another platform that works well for sending people to products, see how to make money on Pinterest without a big following.

Disclosing paid posts: Instagram's label and FTC rules

Instagram's rules. Instagram says: "If you're getting paid in any form for your content, you'll need to add a Paid Partnership label." It also says free trips and gifted products count: "anything received from business partners counts, whether it be money or otherwise" (source). Some products, like drugs and weapons, can't be promoted as branded content. Others, like alcohol, can only be promoted with restrictions. You also shouldn't put pre-, mid- or post-roll ads in videos or audio, or banner ads in videos or images.

FTC rules (U.S.). The FTC's Disclosures 101 for Social Media Influencers says:

  • You must disclose a "material connection" to a brand. That includes personal, family, employment or financial relationships, "such as the brand paying you or giving you free or discounted products or services."
  • Disclosure is your responsibility as the influencer.
  • If a brand gives you free or discounted products or other perks and you then mention one of its products, disclose it even if you weren't asked to mention that product.
  • Disclosures are likely to be missed if they appear only on a profile page, at the end of posts or videos, or behind a "more" click. Don't mix them into a group of hashtags or links.
  • On Instagram Stories, superimpose the disclosure over the picture. In a live stream, repeat it periodically.
  • "Advertisement," "ad" and "sponsored" are clear terms. Avoid "sp," "spon," "collab," and stand-alone terms like "thanks" or "ambassador."
  • Don't assume a platform's disclosure tool is good enough on its own; use it in addition to your own disclosure.
  • If you post from abroad, U.S. law applies if it's reasonably foreseeable that the post will affect U.S. consumers, and foreign laws might also apply.

The FTC also says that if you have no brand relationship and are just telling people about a product you bought and like, you don't need to declare that. A simple routine for paid posts: turn on the Paid Partnership label, start the caption with "Ad" before the "more" cut-off, add the word on screen in Stories and Reels, and repeat it during sponsored Lives.

Taxes on Instagram income

For U.S. readers, the IRS says you must report gig economy income on a tax return even if it comes from part-time or side work, isn't reported on a form like a 1099-K, 1099-MISC, 1099-NEC or W-2, or is paid in any form, including cash, property, goods or virtual currency (IRS Gig Economy Tax Center). Its examples of gig work include "Sell goods online" and "Provide creative or professional services," and it notes the list isn't complete.

Keep records of every payout and of the value of gifted products. If you live elsewhere, check your own tax authority's rules. For how income types are classified, see passive income vs active income.

Which path to start with

Use the facts above to choose where to put your effort first:

  • Below the reported thresholds: start with UGC, affiliate links, direct brand pitches and your own product or service, since Buffer reports no minimum for brand deals, UGC and affiliate work.
  • Past 500 followers and making Reels: check whether Gifts appear in your app.
  • Past 10K followers in a supported country, with content you can keep producing: look at Subscriptions, and remember payouts come on the 21st of the following month.
  • Comfortable going live: test Badges, keeping in mind the $100 payout threshold.
  • Already doing brand deals: add partnership ad pricing to your rate sheet.

Whatever your size, the most dependable answer to how to make money on Instagram is to combine more than one method, as Instagram itself suggests, rather than wait for an invitation to Bonuses.

FAQ

Does Instagram pay for views?

Only through Bonuses, which reward the performance of reels and photos and are limited time and invite-only. Instagram doesn't publish rates in the sources we read.

Do I need a big following to make money on Instagram?

Not for every method. Buffer reports 500 followers for Gifts and 10K for Subscriptions, but no minimum for brand deals, UGC and affiliate marketing. Selling your own products has no Instagram threshold at all. Check the in-app tools in your own account, because requirements can vary by region and over time.

When do Subscriptions pay out?

Instagram says on the 21st of the following month; March earnings, for example, are paid on April 21.

Do gifted products need a Paid Partnership label?

Yes. Instagram says anything received from business partners counts, whether it be money or otherwise, and the FTC treats free or discounted products as a material connection you must disclose.

Do I owe tax if I didn't get a 1099?

In the U.S., yes. The IRS says gig income must be reported even if it isn't on a 1099 or W-2, and even if it's paid in goods or virtual currency.
